items.html: And if you say: we said above that there must not be more than three Sefirot of distance between the vessels and their light, so how did the vessel of Daat descend to Malchut of Beria? The answer is that certainly, where it is possible, it is possible. Now, at first, this one enjoyed and that one did not lack, for at first the vessel enjoyed its light while Daat was below, and the light did not lack either, for even if it were to rise to its place in the Daat of Atzilut, it would have no vessel there at all; therefore it wished to shine into its own vessel, and once it descended, it would not rise again. However, when it saw that there was a form of vessel in its place, closer to its own enjoyment and benefit than to benefiting its own vessel, for now, upon rising above to its place, it has a vessel there, and there it can receive the light for itself from above, from the Emanator, and from Keter, in great closeness, it therefore rose above. This reason suffices for the aspect of the light's benefit for itself. And indeed, regarding the aspect of the loss of its vessel by its descending below into Malchut of Beria, as mentioned, it is not so great a loss, for what we say, that there must be no more than three Sefirot of distance between the light and its vessel, is according to the measure of the three Sefirot of Atzilut, whose measure is great; but in Beria, all ten Sefirot of Beria, their measure is not even equal to the measure of a single Sefira of Atzilut. Therefore it is as though it stands at the head of Beria, for all ten Sefirot of Beria are counted as the measure of a single Sefira.
